cards.title: Can efficient randomized evidence lack a comparably short certain proof?
cards.formal: Are there properties of growing families of finite mathematical objects that can be certified efficiently with arbitrarily high probabilistic confidence, yet have no comparably short certain proofs? The source poses this as a broad question about mathematical evidence; an object encoding, randomized guarantee and proof system must be fixed before it defines a separation to prove.
cards.why: Asks how probabilistic computational evidence compares with certain verification of finite mathematical facts. Its significance depends on distinguishing practical reproducibility, derandomization and proof complexity rather than merging them into one undefined obstacle.
cards.status_note: Full source discussion, primality comparison and subsequent searches checked through 11 September 2026. The source does not formulate one proof system or asymptotic separation, so its broad question cannot receive a single verified open/closed disposition.

progress.text: The deterministic polynomial-time primality theorem rules out primality as an asymptotic example of the proposed randomized-versus-deterministic separation.
The FUN paper raises the broad evidence-versus-proof question in its discussion of reproducible probabilistic diameter bounds.

category_assignment.reason: The central target separates efficient probabilistic certification from certain certification of finite properties.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison of randomized mathematical evidence, deterministic decision and proof length. Existing numerical score retained.

sentences: Random experiments can provide strong evidence for a deterministic property of a finite object.
The source asks whether such evidence can be efficient even when a comparably short certain proof is unavailable.
Efficient deterministic decision, short checkable certificates and short proofs in a chosen calculus are different requirements.
The Rubik experiment and primality example illustrate practical evidence, not established proof-length separations.
A precise object family, evidence guarantee and proof system remain to be selected.

cards.definitions: For a complexity-theoretic formulation, encode an object by a binary string x of length n and represent the property by a language L. A bounded-error randomized polynomial-time decider gives the correct membership answer with probability at least 2/3 on every input; independent repetition can reduce this error to δ with O(log(1/δ)) repetitions. A deterministic polynomial-time decider instead always gives the correct answer. A different notion is a polynomially checkable certificate: a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p satisfy x∈L iff there exists a string π of length at most p(n) with V(x,π)=1. This asks for certificate existence and efficient checking, not for efficiently finding the certificate. A proof-length question in a particular formal calculus additionally fixes that calculus, its axioms and proof encoding. A bound on the probability that an experiment issues a false certificate is a sampling guarantee; it is not automatically a posterior probability that a fixed mathematical statement is false. For one fixed finite object, asymptotic proof-length claims require a growing parameter or a family, since a single statement can be treated as a constant-size instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Select one precise family, evidence protocol, resource scale and sound proof notion, then prove or refute the resulting separation. A large experiment, a small p-value, practical difficulty finding a proof, or a lower bound only for one proof method does not by itself establish absence of all short certificates in a broader model.

context_blocks.title: A deterministic fact can be investigated randomly
context_blocks.text: The diameter of a fixed puzzle graph has one definite value. Random sampling can nevertheless provide a reliable procedure for drawing conclusions about it without exploring the entire graph. The randomness belongs to the procedure, not to the underlying mathematical fact.

context_blocks.title: The motivating experiment is not a proof-length lower bound
context_blocks.text: The paper uses random Rubik states and a solver to support a 36-move upper bound with a controlled sampling-error probability. Its abstract also recalls the independently established 20-move bound. This illustrates the cost of reproducing evidence, rather than an example known to have no short certain proof.

context_blocks.title: Primality does not establish the desired separation
context_blocks.text: Randomized primality testing illustrates the practical usefulness of randomness, but PRIMES is also decidable in deterministic polynomial time by the Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena theorem. It therefore supplies no asymptotic separation of randomized and deterministic polynomial-time decision.

context_blocks.title: Finding a proof and checking one are separate resources
context_blocks.text: A certificate may be short and easy to verify even when nobody knows how to find it quickly. Replacing “no short proof” with “no fast deterministic decision algorithm” changes the question, just as replacing a general certificate with a proof in one fixed calculus does.

cards.title: Explicit superlinear circuit lower bounds with polynomially growing depth
cards.formal: Construct an explicit family f_n:{0,1}^n→{0,1} and constants δ₁,δ₂>0 such that no family of bounded-fan-in, bounded-fan-out Boolean circuits with depth O(n^{δ₁}) and size O(n^{1+δ₂}) computes every f_n exactly. cards.why: A positive result would substantially strengthen lower bounds for general bounded-fan Boolean circuits at depths that grow as a power of the input length. The source uses this target to explain why certain distributed lower bounds may be exceptionally difficult.

category_assignment.reason: The selected conjecture explicitly asks for Boolean circuit size-depth lower bounds; its use as a barrier for distributed lower bounds is downstream.

importance.reason: A strong circuit lower-bound target underlying barriers for distributed subgraph detection. Existing numerical score retained.

sentences: The target is a concrete Boolean-function family that cannot be computed by circuits which are both near-linear in size and polynomially bounded in depth.
Both exponents must exceed their baseline by a fixed positive amount.
The circuits may be nonuniform but must be correct on every input.
The source links sufficiently strong distributed lower bounds to this still-unproved circuit target.
The precise uniform resource requirement behind the word explicit remains to be selected.

cards.definitions: A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n Boolean inputs, Boolean gates and one output. Size counts gates, and depth is the longest input-to-output path. Bounded fan-in and fan-out mean a constant bound independent of n on the number of incoming and outgoing wires at a gate; standard bounded bases, such as AND, OR, NOT and copy gates, differ by constant-factor size and logarithmic/additive depth overheads immaterial to positive polynomial exponents. The circuits are deterministic and nonuniform: different input lengths may use unrelated circuits, with no efficient construction algorithm for the circuits assumed. Exact computation requires C_n(x)=f_n(x) for every x∈{0,1}^n. Once δ₁,δ₂ are fixed, exclusion of the family means that for every fixed fan bound and constants A,B>0, there are arbitrarily large n for which no circuit of depth at most A n^{δ₁} and size at most B n^{1+δ₂} computes f_n. This is a simultaneous depth-and-size restriction; the circuit is not required to be shallow or small separately. An explicitness convention would impose a resource bound on one uniform procedure specifying or evaluating the f_n. Merely asserting that a hard truth table exists does not provide such a convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Fix the intended explicitness requirement, construct a family satisfying it, and prove the simultaneous size/depth exclusion for some positive constants δ₁,δ₂. A counting argument giving unnamed hard functions, a constant-depth lower bound only, or a superlinear bound with no fixed polynomial exponent saving does not meet the stated target.

context_blocks.title: Both resource bounds have to be beaten together
context_blocks.text: For illustration, δ₁=0.01 and δ₂=0.01 would exclude all exact circuits having depth O(n^{0.01}) and size O(n^{1.01}) for the constructed family. These values are illustrative: any fixed positive pair would suffice. A circuit may escape the claimed lower bound by exceeding either limit.

context_blocks.title: An existence proof is easier than an explicit example
context_blocks.text: There are far more Boolean truth tables than circuits with these resources, so counting proves that hard functions exist. The challenge is to identify a uniformly describable family within a meaningful complexity class and establish its lower bound.

context_blocks.title: The source explains a barrier for distributed lower bounds
context_blocks.text: Theorem 29 shows that sufficiently strong round lower bounds for ordered induced-path detection or quantum induced-cycle detection would imply this circuit result. That is a conditional implication between lower bounds, not a circuit separation already proved by the paper.

context_blocks.title: “Explicit” controls which construction counts
context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time evaluator is a much stronger requirement than an unlimited search through truth tables. NP verification and exponential-time evaluation are other common circuit-complexity regimes. Since the source does not select one here, the card records that choice as a remaining formulation issue.

A complete formulation must choose and source that requirement. cards.title: Dimension-independent polyhedral sparsifiers for stochastic integer programs
cards.formal: Can the source’s (1−ε)-approximate stochastic sparsification framework be extended to a specified class of general integer linear programs with degree polynomial in 1/p, 1/ε and explicitly identified structural parameters, but independent of the total number of variables and constraints? The source does not select those structural parameters or formalize the general-ILP activation model.
cards.why: Would extend query-efficient stochastic optimization beyond specialized packing and assignment constraints. The polyhedral measure can capture useful redundancy even when feasible solutions have very different cardinalities.
cards.status_note: Source definition, guarantees, item projection and general extension question checked with the preprint abstract and subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No single invariant or general-ILP benchmark is selected in the source, and no matching universal resolution was located.

sentences: A sparsifier chooses which items to query before learning which independently become available.
It must preserve nearly the full expected optimum while its indicator fits inside a small scaling of the feasible-item polytope.
This degree can stay constant even when the number of queried items grows.
The source proves such bounds for knapsack and assignment models.

cards.definitions: In the source’s packing framework, E is a finite set of items, F⊆2^E is the downward-closed family of feasible item sets, and P_F=conv{1_S:S∈F} is their feasibility polytope. Here 1_S is the 0–1 indicator vector of S; P_F is the convex hull of integer feasible sets, not an arbitrary linear-programming relaxation. Each item independently becomes active with the common known probability p∈(0,1], producing R⊆E. A nonadaptive sparsifier chooses a possibly random query set Q⊆E before seeing R and learns which queried items are active. Degree at most d means 1_Q∈d P_F for every realization of Q; the empty query set can have degree zero. Given a nonnegative objective f on feasible item sets, put OPT(R)=max{f(S):S∈F,S⊆R}. The approximation requirement is E_{Q,R}[OPT(Q∩R)]≥(1−ε)E_R[OPT(R)], with Q independent of the unknown activation realization. For assignment problems, F records which item sets admit some feasible assignment to bins; the actual assignment is chosen after activation is revealed. An ILP ordinarily has integer variables, linear constraints and a linear objective. How such a general instance supplies E,F and independent activation is part of the extension still to be specified.
cards.answer_criterion: Name an ILP class, activation model and structural invariants, then give an efficiently constructible query set with the claimed polyhedral-degree and expected-value bounds independent of dimension, or establish an obstruction within that same specification. A bound allowed to depend on a structural parameter that simply encodes the entire instance size does not give the intended dimension-independent conclusion.

context_blocks.title: Degree measures redundancy, not the number of queried items
context_blocks.text: If every subset of E is feasible, then P_F=[0,1]^E. Querying all n items has degree one, even though it makes n queries. Thus constant degree does not mean a constant number of probes; it means the query set fits into a constant scaling of the feasible-set polytope.

context_blocks.title: Near-optimal information need not solve the optimization problem
context_blocks.text: The sparsifier preserves the expected optimum available among queried active items. Computing that optimum may remain hard. An efficient construction of Q therefore does not imply a polynomial-time near-optimal solution algorithm for every resulting integer program.

context_blocks.title: The source already handles several important packing models
context_blocks.text: Knapsack, multiple knapsack and generalized assignment admit sparsifiers of degree polynomial in inverse activation probability and inverse accuracy, independent of item and constraint counts. The query degree is defined in item space, so assignments and item indicators cannot be interchanged.

context_blocks.title: Expectation is weaker than success on every activation set
context_blocks.text: Some rare activation realizations may lose much of their optimum. The definition compares expected optimal values under independent activation. Requiring a multiplicative approximation for every realization would be a different and stronger problem.

context_blocks.title: The structural parameter must carry specific information
context_blocks.text: A parameter might describe restricted interaction between constraints and variables, but the source’s open question does not pick one. Until it does, there is no proposed universal bound whose validity can be proved or disproved.

statement_review.remaining_issue: A general-ILP extension needs to specify how integer variables become independently activated items, the admissible coefficient signs and domains, the feasibility polytope/projection, and the allowed intrinsic structural parameters. The phrase “intrinsic structural parameters” does not name an invariant or bound its dependence; permitting a parameter that itself equals the dimension would make dimension independence vacuous. The intended efficient construction model and expected versus stronger approximation guarantee must be preserved when selecting a complete extension.

cards.title: One forecaster with the optimal regret rate for every proper loss
cards.formal: For each fixed number K≥2 of outcomes, does there exist one randomized online forecaster A, not given the loss function, such that for every bounded proper loss ℓ its worst-case expected regret satisfies R_A,ℓ(T)≤C_ℓ,K·(1+R*_ℓ,K(T))·(log(T+2))^{c_ℓ,K} for all T≥1, for some constants C_ℓ,K>0 and c_ℓ,K≥0 independent of T? Here R*_ℓ,K is the minimax regret achievable by a forecaster tailored to that particular loss. This spells out the source’s “optimal up to constant or logarithmic factors in T” target; the additive one covers losses with zero or bounded optimal regret.
cards.why: Would establish whether a general-purpose probability forecaster can match every downstream user’s best possible learning rate without knowing that user’s loss. It refines universal sublinear regret into adaptation to the intrinsic difficulty of each scoring rule.
cards.status_note: Full forecasting model, proven simultaneous bounds and concluding question checked with the June arXiv record and subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No loss-universal minimax-rate result or impossibility was located. The displayed minimax comparison makes the asymptotic target explicit.

progress.text: The paper simultaneously achieves logarithmic regret for smooth proper losses and nearly square-root regret for every bounded proper loss, leaving individual-rate optimality for all proper losses open.

cards.definitions: The prediction space is the simplex Δ_K={p∈ℝ^K:p_i≥0,∑p_i=1}. At round t, A chooses a possibly random P_t∈Δ_K from earlier revealed outcomes, then observes y_t∈{e₁,…,e_K}, where e_i is the ith unit vector. The adversary fixes y₁,…,y_T in advance, knowing A but not its random bits. For a measurable loss ℓ:Δ_K×{e₁,…,e_K}→[−1,1], propriety means E_{Y∼p}ℓ(p,Y)≤E_{Y∼p}ℓ(q,Y) for every p,q∈Δ_K; the minimizer need not be unique. Define Reg_A,ℓ(y₁:T)=E_A[∑_{t=1}^T ℓ(P_t,y_t)]−inf_{p∈Δ_K}∑_{t=1}^Tℓ(p,y_t). The expectation is over forecasting randomness, while the comparator is the best single fixed probability prediction in hindsight. Propriety makes the empirical outcome distribution a minimizing comparator. Set R_A,ℓ(T)=sup_{y₁:T}Reg_A,ℓ(y₁:T), and R*_ℓ,K(T)=inf_B R_B,ℓ(T), where B ranges over randomized online prediction strategies allowed to know ℓ,K and T. The desired A may know K and the horizon T, but its predictions are independent of which downstream loss is evaluated. Constants and logarithmic exponents may depend on the fixed loss and K; the asymptotic comparison is in T. This is an expected-regret comparison for each loss, not one simultaneous high-probability event over all losses. The question does not impose a particular polynomial running-time bound or a finite-precision implementation model; the target is the attainable online regret rate.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a loss-independent forecaster and prove the comparison for every bounded proper loss, or show that every such forecaster has some bounded proper loss for which its worst-case expected regret exceeds every allowed logarithmic-factor comparison with that loss’s minimax rate. Achieving Õ(√T) for all losses alone does not settle the question, because some individual losses admit logarithmic or smaller regret.

context_blocks.title: Different users judge the same forecast differently
context_blocks.text: A probability forecast can be used by many downstream decision makers. Proper losses reward reporting the true probability distribution in expectation, but different losses penalize mistakes differently. The forecaster must issue the same P_t before knowing which user’s loss will be used.

context_blocks.title: Worst-case optimal for a class can still be poor for an easy loss

cards.context:
A probability forecast can be used by many downstream decision makers. Proper losses reward reporting the true probability distribution in expectation, but different losses penalize mistakes differently. The forecaster must issue the same P_t before knowing which user’s loss will be used.

For squared loss, logarithmic regret is attainable. A general guarantee of order √T can therefore be much worse than a user could obtain with a loss-specific forecaster. The target adapts to each loss’s own difficulty, rather than just the hardest loss in the class.

The paper gives one efficient algorithm with Õ(K^{5/4}√T) regret for every bounded proper loss and O(β log T+β√K log K) for bounded β-smooth proper losses. It also extends logarithmic guarantees to a broader relative-smoothness class. These are substantial simultaneous guarantees, but do not characterize every individual proper loss.

The hindsight benchmark is one fixed probability vector p, chosen after all outcomes are known. Competing with a different optimal p_t on every round would be a much stronger and generally impossible target under arbitrary outcome sequences.

For each fixed loss, average regret over A’s own randomization must have the required rate against every fixed outcome sequence. The statement does not claim that a single realized random trajectory satisfies all loss bounds with high probability.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
